AI-Generated (186 words): Maybe a trip once showed you a love you didn't know was possible, or a peace that just kept going. Whatever it was, it matters. It can stay a reference point, with no need to keep chasing it. Feeling it once on a psychedelic is still a long way from finding it sober, though, and finding it now and then is a long way from living in it day to day.
The beautiful state can become a hook, too. Say you had one amazing night on a psychedelic, or a dream like that, and now it's the bar, so regular life starts to feel like failing. How intense or beautiful it was doesn't prove that what you saw really happened, or that you're done healing. I'd look at what's changed once it wears off. Are you more honest, more protective of your little one, more reliable, all that?
And if your little one still can't take the love in? Maybe a protective part doesn't trust it yet, or they learned long ago that love comes with strings attached.

AI-Generated (146 words): ## How This Relates to IFS
So how's this different from Internal Family Systems (IFS)? Honestly, in a lot of ways it isn't. IFS recognizes protective parts too, and teaches people to approach them without shame or a fight, so "meet the protector first" fits right in. But my reparenting method diverges from IFS at an important point. In standard IFS, the healer is the Self, a calm, compassionate source that's supposed to show up once your parts "unblend." For me it's the inner adult you build and practice being, that one grown-up doing all three jobs.
And what if that calm inner source just won't show up for you? That's where borrowed adulthood comes in. Maybe you borrow one grown-up job from a friend, or from a plan you've made, and take it in bit by bit.

AI-Generated (277 words): A grown-up you can trust gets built through care and boundaries, and through action and direction.
IFS calls these wounded young parts "exiles." I find that pathologizing. I prefer to speak of a child who needs parenting and integration, rather than naming them by their wounded or excluded condition. IFS "unburdening," often done after witnessing a part's origin story, can be powerful. But it can also get dramatic, with a lot of focus on memories and plenty of room for suggestion, and that can knock people off balance, especially if they tend to dissociate (DID-like fragmentation included) or to spiritually bypass.
And then there's the map itself. Managers, firefighters, exiles, polarized parts, legacy burdens, Self-energy, guides, new subparts... how many parts is that now? It can turn into a maze. Some practitioners use the model gently, and others seem to leave people more fragmented while trying to fix the fragmenting. Having institutes and certifications behind a framework doesn't make it any more true, or safer for that matter.
Before choosing a therapist, get to know the strengths and pitfalls of IFS and reparenting. Could an IFS therapist help? They may, if they're skilled and grounded. You'd want one who's trauma-informed and doesn't put ideas in your head, especially one who understands dissociation. For your little one's pain, or for shame, a good reparenting therapist may fit better. The same goes for attachment wounds or abandoning yourself, or not having an inner adult you can count on.
